<reflection>
- The first experiment successfully separated the models into distinct tiers. The top tier consists of M6, M8, M7, and M3, all of which have NLL values around -23.6, significantly better than the standard Michaelis-Menten model (M1, NLL -14.0).
- These top models all introduce some form of non-linearity or delay to the initial kinetics: M6 and M8 involve catalyst activation (creating a lag phase), M3 involves catalyst dimerization (second-order dependence on catalyst), and M7 involves a second substrate binding step (second-order dependence on substrate).
- My aim to establish a baseline and cluster the mechanisms was achieved.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
To distinguish between the top four mechanisms (M6, M8, M7, M3), we need to probe the reaction's dependence on both catalyst and substrate concentrations simultaneously. 
By significantly lowering the catalyst concentration (from 0.1 to 0.01), we can differentiate the catalyst activation and dimerization models. In M3 (dimerization), the active species concentration scales with [cat]^2, so the rate will drop precipitously. In M6 (first-order activation), the active fraction is independent of [cat], so the rate scales linearly. In M8 (activation with ligand dissociation, cat <=> cat* + L), the degree of dissociation increases at lower concentrations, meaning the active fraction will be higher than in M6, leading to a sub-linear drop in rate.
By simultaneously lowering the substrate concentration (from 2.0 to 0.5), we can test M7. In M7, the rate-determining step involves a second substrate molecule (catS2). Lowering [S] will disproportionately reduce the rate compared to models with standard Michaelis-Menten substrate dependence (M6, M8, M3).
This combination of low [cat] and low [S] will pull the predictions of the top four models in completely different directions, maximizing the information gained and reducing uncertainty across the entire set of plausible mechanisms.
</hypothesis>
